Arching the lower back → Bring your ribs down and reduce the load

ipuclari: Lift your hips into an inverted V; hands shoulder-width apart.
Lower the top of your head slightly in front of your hands to form a triangle.
Raising your feet onto a box brings the load closer to a handstand push-up.
Flare your elbows 45° forward and out, not straight to the sides.
hatalar: Lowering the head straight down between the hands → Lower your head in front of your hands to form a triangle
Dropping the hips back into a regular push-up → Keep your hips over your shoulders

ipuclari: Kick up into a handstand facing the wall; hands 10–20 cm from the wall, shoulder-width apart.
Lower the top of your head towards the floor in front of your hands to form a triangle, then press.
Put a cushion under your head; at first, work only the slow lowering (negative).
Low reps, long rest; end the set when your shoulders tire.
hatalar: Banging the head hard on the floor → Use a cushion, lower slowly and start with negatives
Arching the lower back excessively → Squeeze your glutes and abs and bring your ribs down
Falling out of the handstand when tired → Learn a safe exit (turning to the side) and use the wall

ipuclari: Lie under a bar at waist height and grip it shoulder-width apart.
Form a straight line from heels to head; pull your chest to the bar and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
The more upright your body, the easier it is; parallel to the floor with feet raised is harder.
Because the load on the lower back is low, it's a good pulling choice when your back is sensitive.
hatalar: Hips dropping → Squeeze your glutes and keep your body straight
Shrugging the shoulders to the ears → Pull your shoulder blades back and down

ipuclari: Hold the straps and lean back; the further forward your feet, the harder it is.
Pull your chest towards your hands, elbows close to your torso or flared at 45°.
Return slowly and straighten your arms fully.
An adjustable, back-friendly first pulling exercise for beginners.
hatalar: Breaking at the hips → Keep your body straight
Not checking the anchor point → Test the door or post anchor first

ipuclari: Grip the bar shoulder-width apart, arms straight, feet off the floor.
At first, take some of the load with your feet for support.
Build the time gradually: from 10–15 s up to 30–60 s.
Let go if you feel a pinch in the shoulder or a sense it might slip out.
hatalar: Jumping or dropping off the bar → Step down onto a box
Hanging fully passive despite shoulder instability → Keep your shoulder blades slightly active and shorten the time

ipuclari: Hanging with straight arms, pull only your shoulder blades down and back; your body rises a few cm.
Don't bend your elbows; the movement is in the shoulder girdle.
Hold for 1–2 s at the top, release slowly.
It teaches the first phase of the pull-up and the lower traps.
hatalar: Bending the elbows to pull → Keep your arms fully straight
Swinging → Keep your legs still and go slowly

ipuclari: Use a box to get your chin above the bar, then step off the box.
Lower under control over 3–5 s; finish when your arms are fully straight.
Few reps (3–5), many sets; eccentric loading increases muscle soreness.
End the set the moment you can't control the lowering.
hatalar: Dropping down fast → Keep counting the descent (3–5 s)
Doing too many reps → 3–5 reps per set

ipuclari: Band under your foot or knee; on the machine, choose a counterweight.
Get your chin above the bar, lower under control.
Reduce the assistance over the weeks: a thinner band or less counterweight.
A band helps most at the bottom and least at the top; train the top position separately.
hatalar: Band slipping off the foot → Tie the band securely to the bar and centre your foot
Half reps → Straighten your arms fully and get your chin above the bar

ipuclari: Palms facing away, grip slightly wider than shoulder width.
Pull your shoulder blades down and bring your chest to the bar; get your chin above the bar.
Straighten your arms fully at the bottom; don't let your shoulders stay up by your ears.
Latissimus activity is 117–130% MVIC; the most effective bodyweight pull.
Progression: once reps go up, move to a weight belt or one-arm progressions.
hatalar: Swinging out reps with kipping → Strict reps, legs still
Reaching the head forward to get the chin over the bar → Bring your chest to the bar
Dropping off the bar → Lower the last rep under control too

ipuclari: Pull your chest towards the bar with an explosive pull-up, and turn your wrists over the bar as it reaches your lower chest.
After the transition, press like a dip to straighten your arms.
First get solid chest-to-bar pull-ups and straight bar dips; practise the transition on a low bar with foot support.
Low reps, full rest; don't attempt it when tired.
hatalar: Arms out of sync, one side going over first (chicken wing) → Practise a symmetrical transition on a low bar
Uncontrolled kipping → Learn it with strict form first
Forcing reps when tired → End the set at 1–3 reps

ipuclari: Keep your elbows fixed at your sides; don't let your shoulders drift forward.
Breathe out as you lift, lower over 2–3 s.
Choose a weight you can lift without swinging your torso.
A straight bar forces the wrists into full supination; if your wrists or elbows hurt, use an EZ bar.
hatalar: Swinging the torso to lift → Reduce the load and lean your back against a wall
Dropping the weight with the elbow fully stretched at the bottom → Lower under control and stop softly at the bottom
Continuing despite wrist pain on a straight bar → Switch to an EZ bar or dumbbells

ipuclari: Keep your elbows fixed at your sides; don't let your shoulders drift forward.
Breathe out as you lift, lower over 2–3 s.
Choose a weight you can lift without swinging your torso.
The cable gives resistance through the whole movement; good for a controlled start with a light load.
hatalar: Swinging the torso to lift → Reduce the load and lean your back against a wall
Dropping the weight with the elbow fully stretched at the bottom → Lower under control and stop softly at the bottom

ipuclari: Pin your elbows to your sides; only your forearms move.
Straighten your arms fully at the bottom; at the top, don't let your elbows go past 90°.
A rope handle is easier on the wrists.
When your shoulder is sensitive, it's one of the triceps options that puts the least load on the shoulder.
hatalar: Leaning forward and pushing down with body weight → Stand upright and reduce the load
Elbows moving back and forth → Keep your elbows fixed

ipuclari: Lower the dumbbell behind your head with both hands; elbows pointing forward, close to your ears.
The long head of the triceps is stretched in this position; with cables, 1.4 times more triceps growth was seen over 12 weeks than with the arm at your side.
Doing it seated with back support protects your lower back.
Start with a lighter weight; the load used overhead is ~35% lower.
hatalar: Arching the lower back → Brace your abs or do it seated
Flaring the elbows out → Keep your elbows forward and in

ipuclari: Lie on your back and hold the bar straight above your chest with an EZ grip.
Bending only at the elbows, lower the bar to just above your forehead or behind your head.
Keeping your arms angled slightly back stretches the triceps more.
Moderate load, 8–15 reps; avoid heavy single attempts.
hatalar: Flaring the elbows out → Keep your elbows shoulder-width apart, pointing at the ceiling
Lowering a heavy weight without control → Reduce the load and use a spotter

ipuclari: Elbows slightly bent; raise your arms out to the side and slightly forward (scapular plane, ~30°).
Raise to shoulder height; higher works the traps and can pinch the shoulder.
Thumbs pointing slightly up; don't turn them in as if 'emptying a jug'.
Light weight, 12–20 reps; lift with control, not speed.
hatalar: Raising with the arm turned in (thumbs down) → Keep your thumbs pointing slightly up
Swinging the torso to lift heavy weight → Reduce the load
Shrugging the shoulders to the ears → Keep your shoulders down

ipuclari: Raise your arm forward to shoulder height; a neutral grip (thumbs up) is easier on the shoulder.
Torso upright, lower back still.
The front delts already work a lot in presses; you may not need extra in your programme.
Light weight, 10–15 reps.
hatalar: Raising the arm far above shoulder height → Stop at shoulder height
Throwing the lower back back to lift → Reduce the load and stand tall

ipuclari: Do it on an incline bench with chest support or on a reverse pec deck.
Arms slightly bent, open them out and back; stop at shoulder level.
Prone horizontal abduction with external rotation works the rear delts and the middle-lower traps a lot.
Light weight, 12–20 reps.
hatalar: Rounding the lower back in a bent-over standing position → Use chest support
Shrugging the shoulder blades and pulling with the traps → Keep your shoulders down and reduce the load

ipuclari: Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, hold for 1 s, lower slowly.
Don't roll your shoulders; circular movement adds no extra benefit.
Head neutral, chin tucked.
If your grip is weak, you can use straps.
hatalar: Rolling the shoulders forward and back → Move straight up and down
Pushing the head forward → Eyes forward, chin tucked

ipuclari: Elbow bent at 90°, at your side; put a rolled towel between your elbow and your body.
Rotate your forearm outward without letting your elbow leave your side; return slowly.
Side-lying dumbbell external rotation works the infraspinatus and teres minor the most.
Light load, 15–20 reps, 2–3 times a week; keep pain at or below 3/10.
hatalar: Moving the elbow away from the body → Don't drop the towel roll
Rotating the torso to gain movement → Keep your torso still

ipuclari: Rest your forearm on your knee or a bench, with your wrist hanging over the edge.
Palm up works the flexors; palm down (reverse wrist curl) works the extensors.
Light weight, 15–20 reps, slow lowering.
The slow lowering of the reverse wrist curl is similar to the loading used in tennis elbow rehabilitation.
hatalar: Swinging a heavy weight fast → Light weight, controlled tempo
Increasing the load despite pain → Keep pain at or below 3/10 and make sure it isn't worse the next day

ipuclari: Elbows under your shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels.
Squeeze your glutes lightly and keep your abs tight without holding your breath; breathe normally.
Beginners start with 3–4 sets of 10–15 s holds and build the time gradually; once 60 s is easy, move to a harder variation.
Push your shoulder blades slightly forward and tilt your pelvis slightly back (posterior tilt): this version clearly increases abdominal activity.
hatalar: Hips dropping, lower back arching → Squeeze your glutes and draw your ribs towards your pelvis
Hips raised too high → Keep shoulders, hips and heels in the same line
Holding your breath → Take short, steady breaths

ipuclari: In a high plank (hands on the floor), set your feet shoulder-width apart; the wider they are, the easier it gets.
Tap the opposite shoulder with one hand without letting your hips rotate to the side.
Go slowly: 1–2 s per tap; 2–3 sets of 10–20 taps.
hatalar: Hips swaying side to side → Widen your feet, squeeze your glutes and slow down
Support shoulder collapsing → Push the floor away and move your shoulder blade forward

ipuclari: Start in a forearm plank; place one hand, then the other, on the floor to rise into a high plank, then come back down in the same order.
Widen your feet slightly; keep your hips from shifting sideways as much as possible.
Do 5 reps leading with the right hand, then 5 leading with the left; 2–3 sets.
Covers both variations: rising and lowering one hand at a time, and both hands together (the second one requires pushing power).
hatalar: Hips rotating and rising a lot → Widen your feet and slow the tempo
Dropping hard onto the elbows → Use a soft surface and lower under control

ipuclari: On all fours, hands under your shoulders, knees under your hips.
Extend one arm and the opposite leg parallel to the floor, hold for 5–10 s, bring them back.
Keep your back flat and don't let your hip open to the side; 6–10 reps per side.
hatalar: Lifting the leg too high and arching the lower back → Lift the leg only to hip height
Hip rotating to the side → Imagine a glass on your back and go slower

ipuclari: Lie on your back; press your lower back into the floor and lift your shoulders and legs off the floor.
Arms overhead, legs straight; if it's too hard, bend your knees or bring your arms to your sides.
3–4 sets of 15–30 s; once 60 s is easy, move to the hollow rock or V-up.
hatalar: Lower back lifting off the floor → Drop to an easier version: knees bent, arms at your sides
Pulling the neck forward → Chin slightly tucked, eyes on your knees

ipuclari: Start on your knees (on a soft mat); push the wheel forward, letting your hips and torso extend together.
Stop where your lower back starts to arch and pull back; your range will increase over time.
2–4 sets of 5–12 reps; the standing version (knees off the floor) is advanced.
hatalar: Lower back arching (sagging) → Shorten the range of motion and squeeze your abs and glutes
Leaving the hips behind and reaching only with the arms → Move your hips and shoulders forward together
Bending at the lower back to pull back → Come back with your abs braced

ipuclari: Lie on your side; elbow under your shoulder, lift your hips to form a straight line from head to feet.
Easier version: knees bent. Harder version: lift your top leg or raise your feet.
3–4 sets of 10–30 s per side; compare the times for both sides.
hatalar: Hips drifting back or dropping → Push your hips forward into a straight line
Shoulder collapsing towards the ear → Push the floor away with your elbow, shoulder down

ipuclari: Lie on your back, knees bent; keep your hands on your chest or under your lower back (McGill curl-up).
Lift only your shoulders a few cm off the floor; keep your lower back down, hold for 1–2 s, lower.
2–4 sets of 10–15 reps; keep the total number of flexion reps per session limited (no more than ≈60) and allow 48 hours between sessions.
hatalar: Pulling the head with your hands → Cross your hands over your chest or rest them lightly beside your head
Lifting the whole torso (turning it into a sit-up) → Lift only your shoulder blades
Doing it right after getting up in the morning → Do it at least 1 hour after getting up

ipuclari: Knees bent, feet on the floor; roll your torso up one vertebra at a time towards your knees, lower under control.
Anchoring your feet increases the hip flexors' contribution; to focus on your abs, don't anchor them.
2–3 sets of 8–15 reps; slow tempo (≈2 s).
hatalar: Pulling the neck with your hands → Hands on your chest
Doing it fast and with momentum → Slow tempo
Doing it with high reps (100+) → Add weight and stay at 6–15 reps

ipuclari: Hold the dumbbell at your chest with both hands; as you come up in the sit-up, press the dumbbell forward/up at the top.
Bring the dumbbell back to your chest and lower under control.
Start with a light weight; 2–3 sets of 10–20.
hatalar: Being thrown around by the dumbbell's weight → Reduce the weight and slow the tempo
Slamming the lower back on the floor on the way down → Lower under control

ipuclari: On your back, shoulders slightly off the floor; pull one knee in towards the opposite elbow while the other leg extends.
Let the rotation come from your torso, don't yank your elbow; switch slowly and under control.
2–3 sets of 10–15 per side.
hatalar: Pulling the head with your hands → Hands resting lightly beside your head
Tempo too fast → 1–2 s per rep

ipuclari: Standing, hands behind your head or overhead; pull one knee out and up and touch the same-side elbow to the knee (side crunch).
Front variation: start with arms overhead, pull your knee up and bring your hands together under the knee.
Hold on to a wall for balance if needed; 15–25 per side, or sets of 50.
hatalar: Standing knee caving in → Bend the standing knee slightly and keep your hips still
Collapsing the torso forward → Stand tall and start the movement from the knee and obliques

ipuclari: On your back, hands at your sides or under your hips; raise your legs, straight or slightly bent, towards the ceiling.
On the way down, stop just above the point where your lower back lifts off the floor; lifting your hips slightly off the floor at the end puts more work on your abs.
2–3 sets of 8–15.
hatalar: Lower back arching on the way down → Bend your knees or cut the lowering short halfway
Swinging the legs → Lower slowly

ipuclari: Hang from the bar; pull your shoulders slightly down and draw your knees to your chest without swinging.
At the top, tilt your pelvis slightly up (curl your hips), then lower slowly.
If your grip is weak, use arm slings; 2–4 sets of 8–15.
hatalar: Swinging for momentum → Pause after each rep and lower slowly
Hanging passively with the shoulders sunk into the ears → Active hang: shoulders down

ipuclari: Hang from the bar and raise your legs, kept straight, to at least parallel to the floor (advanced: feet to the bar).
Pause after each rep to stop the swing; take 2–3 s to lower.
2–4 sets of 5–12.
hatalar: Swinging with momentum → Slow tempo, active hang
Forcing straight legs without enough hamstring flexibility → Start with knee raises, then half-bent legs

ipuclari: On your back, hips and knees at 90°; curl your pelvis to lift your hips off the floor, bringing your knees to your chest.
Lower slowly; don't swing your legs.
To make it harder, use an incline bench (head up); 2–3 sets of 10–15.
hatalar: Swinging the legs for momentum → Keep the movement small and slow
Pushing by pressing the neck into the floor → Arms on the floor, neck relaxed

ipuclari: From the hollow position, lift your arms and straight legs at the same time and reach your hands towards your feet.
Lower slowly; don't let your lower back slam onto the floor.
Easier version: tuck-up (knees bent). 2–3 sets of 6–12.
hatalar: Swinging up → Drop to tuck-ups and slow the tempo
Lower back arching on the way down → Hold the hollow position

ipuclari: Sit and lean your torso back ~45°, knees bent; bring your hands (or a weight) from one side to the other.
Let the rotation come from your rib cage, not your arms; start with your feet on the floor.
2–3 sets of 10–15 per side; light load.
hatalar: Swinging fast with a weight → Light load, slow tempo
Rounding the back → Keep your chest open

ipuclari: Sit upright (on a bench or the floor); hold the dumbbell in one hand and move it forward and back and in circles, or do halos around your head with both hands.
Keep your torso upright and still; let the movement come from the shoulder.
Light load; 10–20 per side/direction.
hatalar: Torso swaying with the weight → Reduce the load and keep your abs braced
Arching the lower back during the halo → Keep your ribs down

ipuclari: Stand side-on to a wall; bring the ball to the side of your back hip and throw it into the wall with a rotation that starts from your hips.
Let your back foot pivot (heel lifts); power flows from your legs and hips to your torso, then your arms.
Explosive work: 3–5 sets of 3–6 throws per side, full rest between sets; 2–4 kg ball.
hatalar: Throwing with the arms only → Start the movement from your hips
Keeping the feet fixed and twisting at the lower back → Pivot on your back foot and let your hips rotate
Too many reps when tired → Few reps, full rest

ipuclari: Attach the cable to a high pulley (high to low) or low pulley (low to high); hold it with both hands.
Let your hips and rib cage rotate together; your back foot pivots.
Controlled power: 2–3 sets of 8–12 per side.
hatalar: Rotating only from the lower back with the hips fixed → Pivot on your back foot and rotate your hips
Bending the arms to pull → Arms long, let your torso do the work

ipuclari: Hold the kettlebells in front of your shoulders (rack position), elbows close to your body.
Ribs down, don't let your lower back arch; keep breathing.
2–4 sets of 20–40 m.
hatalar: Leaning back and arching the lower back → Pull your ribs down and reduce the load
Elbows flaring out → Keep your elbows in

ipuclari: Lock the weight overhead at full arm's length; biceps in line with your ear.
Ribs down, no lower-back arch; walk slowly.
One or both arms; 2–4 sets of 15–30 m.
hatalar: Not fully straightening the arm and carrying the weight in front → Work on shoulder mobility first; reduce the load
Arching the lower back to compensate → Brace your abs and bring your ribs down

ipuclari: Sit on the floor, hands behind your hips with fingers pointing forward (or to the sides), knees bent.
Lift your hips until your torso and thighs form a flat table; hold for 1–2 s, lower.
Can be done with your hands raised (on a coffee table or bench); 2–3 sets of 10–20.
hatalar: Shoulders dropping forward and sinking into the ears → Open your chest and pull your shoulder blades back and down
Stopping the hips halfway → Squeeze your glutes and extend fully

ipuclari: On all fours, round your back as you breathe out (cat) and open your chest forward as you breathe in (cow).
Slow and rhythmic within a pain-free range; 1–2 sets of 8–12 reps.
Can be used as a warm-up or as a break exercise after long sitting.
hatalar: Forcing into a painful end range → Stay within a pain-free range
Moving only from the neck → Start from the pelvis and move one vertebra at a time

ipuclari: Take a long lunge forward; back knee on the floor or off it, place the same-side hand inside your front foot.
Rotate your rib cage by opening your inside arm to the ceiling; then send your hips back to stretch the back of your front leg.
3–5 reps per side, 2–3 s in each position; part of a dynamic warm-up.
hatalar: Dropping the back knee onto a hard floor → Use a mat or keep your knee off the floor
Forcing the rotation from the lower back → Rotate from your rib cage, hips still

ipuclari: Sit on the floor; front leg at 90° at the hip and knee, back leg also at 90° out to the side.
Keep your torso upright and lean slightly over your front leg (external rotation), then turn your knees to the other side (internal rotation).
5–10 switches per side or 20–30 s holds per position.
hatalar: Forcing it without hand support and rounding the back → Support yourself with your hands behind you
Continuing despite pain inside the knee → Reduce the angle or use a cushion

ipuclari: Lie on your side, hips and knees at 90°, arms stacked in front of you.
Sweep your top arm over towards the ceiling and open it behind you, with your eyes following your hand; keep your knees on the floor.
8–10 slow reps per side, 2–3 s at the end point.
hatalar: Knees separating and hips rotating → Press your knees together, with a cushion between them if needed
Forcing the arm to the floor → Stay within a pain-free range

ipuclari: Hold the stick with a wide grip in front of your hips; keeping your arms straight, take it over your head to behind your back and back again.
Find the narrowest grip you can pass through pain-free; narrow it over time.
Behind-the-back and overhead cross variations, 3×45 s a day; retest after 2 weeks.
hatalar: Forcing it through with a narrow grip and bending the elbows → Widen your grip
Arching the lower back to compensate → Keep your ribs down

ipuclari: Rest your forearms on the wall (facing the wall), little-finger side against the wall.
As you slide your forearms up the wall, rotate your shoulder blades forward and up; lower slowly.
2–3 sets of 10–15; the back-to-the-wall version also tests shoulder mobility.
hatalar: Shrugging the shoulders to the ears → Neck long, shoulders down
Arching the lower back → Pull your ribs towards the wall/down

ipuclari: Feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes turned slightly out; go as deep as you can with your heels down.
Push your knees slightly out with your elbows and lift your chest; if needed, hold on to a post or put support under your heels.
1–3 min in total, split into parts (e.g. 3×30–60 s).
hatalar: Heels lifting → Put support under your heels and widen your feet
Knees caving inward → Push your knees in line with your feet

ipuclari: Arms out to the sides; start with small circles and gradually make them bigger. Both forwards and backwards.
Don't shrug your shoulders up to your ears.
10–15 per direction; a warm-up before upper-body training. A standing overhead reach stretch can also be added to this warm-up.
hatalar: Big, fast circles through a painful range → Stay in a pain-free range, under control

ipuclari: Sit upright; slowly move your head forward and back, turn it left and right, and tilt your ear towards your shoulder.
Go to a pain-free end range in each direction and hold for 2–3 s; add chin tucks.
5–10 per direction; during the day, especially after long periods at a screen or desk.
hatalar: Turning the head fast or rolling it in circles → Slowly and in one plane
Pushing into pain or numbness spreading into the arm → Stop; if symptoms spread into the arm, see a specialist

ipuclari: Hold on to a wall; grab one ankle and bring your heel towards your glutes.
Knees side by side, pelvis tilted slightly back; don't let your lower back arch.
2–3 × 20–30 s per side.
hatalar: Letting the knee drift out to the side or arching the lower back → Knees side by side, squeeze your glutes
Bending fully despite knee pain → Loop a towel around your foot and reduce the angle

ipuclari: Front leg bent in front of you, back leg long behind; hips close to the floor and level.
Put a cushion under your hip; lean your torso forward to increase the stretch on the outside of the hip.
2 × 30–60 s per side. Easier version: lying figure-4 stretch.
hatalar: Front knee twisting and hurting on the inside → Bring your front foot closer to your hips or switch to the figure-4
Hips tipping to the side → Support under your hip

ipuclari: Rest your forearm on the door frame with your elbow at shoulder height (or slightly above).
Step forward with the same-side foot and move your chest through the doorway; the stretch should be in your chest, not a pinch at the front of your shoulder.
2–3 × 30 s per side.
hatalar: Shoulder sliding forward and causing joint pain → Pull your shoulder blade back and down and reduce the angle
Arching the lower back → Brace your abs

ipuclari: Knees on the floor, sit your hips back towards your heels, reach your arms forward and rest your forehead on the floor.
Knees apart targets the hips and lats more; knees together targets the lower back more.
30–60 s with relaxed breathing; 1–3 reps.
hatalar: Sitting all the way back despite knee pain → Put a cushion between your hips and heels

ipuclari: Bring your arm across the front of your chest and gently pull above the elbow with your other hand.
Keep your shoulder blade still; the side-lying version (shoulder blade on the floor) may be more effective.
On the restricted side, 5 × 30 s a day (McClure protocol).
hatalar: Pulling despite a pinching pain at the front of the shoulder → Bring the arm across a little lower and use less force

ipuclari: Stand on one foot, standing knee slightly bent; if needed, have something nearby to hold on to.
Progressions: eyes closed, soft surface, head turns, throwing and catching a ball.
Effective dose (young healthy adults): 21–40 s holds, 2 sets per exercise, 11–15 min sessions, 3 sessions a week, for 11–12 weeks.
hatalar: Hip dropping to the side → Keep your pelvis level and squeeze your outer hip
Locking the knee fully → Knee slightly bent

ipuclari: Stand on one foot; with the free foot, reach as far as you can forward, back-inward and back-outward, touch lightly and return.
Don't let the standing heel lift; keep the knee in line with your foot.
3–5 reaches per direction, 2–3 rounds per side; note the difference between the two sides.
hatalar: Putting weight on the free foot → Let only the toes touch lightly
Standing knee caving in → Keep your knee in line with your toes

ipuclari: Stand up; sit down cross-legged on the floor without using your hands or knees, then stand back up the same way.
If it's hard, start with support from one hand or knee; reduce the support over time.
5–10 reps, 2–3 sets; practise regularly to maintain muscle strength and mobility as you age.
hatalar: Dropping down onto the knees → Lower slowly, using your hand for support if needed
Bending the torso excessively to avoid falling forward → Reach your arms forward, weight over your midfoot

ipuclari: On your back, weight locked out towards the ceiling in one arm; same-side knee bent. Eyes on the weight the whole time.
Sequence: up to your elbow → up to your hand → lift your hips → sweep your back leg through underneath onto your knee → stand up; come back down in the same order.
Learn it first without weight (or balancing a shoe); 1–5 slow reps per side.
hatalar: Elbow of the weighted arm bending → Keep the arm locked and reduce the load
Taking your eyes off the weight → Eyes on the weight
Skipping stages and rushing up → Pause at each stage

ipuclari: Swing your arms back, hinge at the hips and explode forward and up.
On landing, feet hip-width apart, hips back, torso leaning forward; stick the landing for 2 s.
3–5 sets × 3–5 reps; increase the distance without your technique breaking down.
Non-slip, slightly forgiving surface (grass, wooden floor, rubber) and supportive shoes; avoid concrete and asphalt.
hatalar: Landing stiff-legged on your heels → Land on your midfoot, bending your hips and knees
Falling forward on landing → Reduce the distance; jump only as far as you can stick
Knees caving inward → Knees in line with your feet

ipuclari: Jump straight up on the spot and pull your knees to your chest in the air; thighs parallel to the floor.
Land softly, rolling from the balls of your feet to your midfoot, and jump again straight away.
As a screen: do it continuously for 10 s and count the six faults by eye or on video.
2–4 sets × 5–8 reps.
hatalar: Knees caving inward → Slow down; keep your knees in line with your feet, and go back to squat jumps if needed
Feet landing narrow or staggered → Feet shoulder-width apart, touching down at the same time
Folding the torso forward instead of pulling the knees to the chest → Less height but an upright torso
Hard, noisy landings → Stop if you can't land softly

ipuclari: First hop with both feet from side to side over a line on the floor; then move to one foot.
Short, quick contacts; keep your knee in line with your foot and your torso upright.
On one foot, stick each landing first, then do them back to back.
hatalar: Ankle rolling outward (inversion) → Shorten the distance; land on the middle of your foot and control it from the hip
Knee caving inward → Squeeze your outer hip and keep your knee over your foot
Throwing the torso to the side → Shoulders still, let only your legs move

ipuclari: Don't jump off the box — step forward and drop; land on both feet and explode up as quickly as possible.
Start with a low box (20–30 cm); if your ground contact time gets longer, the box is too high.
First learn the landing with just 'drop and stick' (depth drop).
3–5 sets × 3–5 reps, full rest.
People over 100 kg shouldn't use a box higher than 45 cm (NSCA).
hatalar: Box too high → A box low enough that contact stays short and the jump stays high
Heels slamming and knees caving on landing → Land on the balls of your feet, knees in line with your feet
Doing it when tired or without warming up → Do it at the start of the session, fresh

ipuclari: Run with exaggerated long strides, leaping from one leg to the other on each step.
Let your foot land close to under your hips with short contact; drive the opposite arm and knee forward hard.
Start short (15–20 m) and submaximal; then increase the distance and intensity.
3–6 reps × 20–30 m, walk back.
hatalar: Landing with the foot far in front of the body → Bring your foot down under your hips
Landing on the heel → Land on your mid-forefoot
Continuing when fatigued → Stop when stride quality drops

ipuclari: Jump sideways off one foot and land on the other; let your back foot stay crossed behind.
On landing, hips back, knee over your foot; at first, stick each landing for 1–2 s.
Increase the distance over time, then do them back to back in a rhythm.
3 sets × 6–10 reps in each direction.
hatalar: Knee caving in on landing → Squeeze your outer hip and keep the distance short
Ankle rolling outward → Land on your whole foot and slow down
Torso tipping to the side → Chest forward, torso still

ipuclari: Jump up from a split squat stance; switch legs in the air or land in the same stance.
On landing, front knee over your foot; let the back knee bend without hitting the floor.
Start with 'split jumps in place' without switching legs.
3 sets × 4–8 reps per leg.
hatalar: Front knee caving inward → Front knee pointing towards your second toe
Back knee hitting the floor → Control the depth and make the jump smaller
Narrow stance on a single line → Feet hip-width apart, on two separate rails

ipuclari: On the spot or moving forward slowly, quickly pull your heels up towards your glutes.
Let your knee point down; light contact on the balls of your feet.
In the warm-up, 2–3 × 20 s or 15–20 m.
hatalar: Folding the torso forward → Torso upright
Lifting the knee forward → Thigh vertical, only the lower leg moves

ipuclari: Start standing or in a half crouch; torso leaning forward, first steps short with a powerful push.
Let your foot land under or slightly behind your hips; swing your arms powerfully.
First warm up for 10–15 min: easy jogging, dynamic stretches, A-skips, 2–3 build-up runs.
Full rest between reps: generally about 1 min for every 10 m (expert consensus); stop when your speed drops.
hatalar: Maximal start without warming up → Warm up gradually, with runs starting at 70–80%
Standing up too early → Torso leaning forward for the first 5–10 m
Reaching the foot forward to land → Bring your foot down under your hips

ipuclari: Build up speed gradually over 20–30 m, then hold a 10–30 m top-speed zone, then slow down gradually.
Upright torso, high knees, short contact with the foot under your hips; shoulders relaxed.
3–6 reps; full rest of 2–4 min.
First warm up for 10–15 min: easy jogging, dynamic stretches, A-skips, 2–3 build-up runs.
hatalar: Doing it when tired or at the end of a session → At the start of the session, fresh
Overstriding → Increase your step rate and bring your foot down under you
Tense shoulders and face → Relaxed but fast

ipuclari: On a moderate hill (about 5–10% gradient), run hard for 8–15 s and walk back down.
Torso leaning slightly into the hill, short powerful steps, arms active.
4–10 reps; walk down and rest fully.
First warm up for 10–15 min: easy jogging, dynamic stretches, A-skips, 2–3 build-up runs.
hatalar: Hill too steep → A gradient where you can keep your running stride
Running back down the hill → Walk down
Rising too high onto your toes → Push from your mid-forefoot and hips

ipuclari: Arms straight or bent, torso leaning 45° forward and straight.
Push from the balls of your feet with short, powerful steps; knee in line with your foot.
For speed: light-to-moderate load, 10–20 m. For conditioning: heavy load, 20–30 m.
4–8 reps; 60–180 s between reps.
hatalar: Lower back rounding or arching → Keep your torso rigid like a plank
Crawling with an overly heavy load → For speed work, choose a load that doesn't slow you down too much
Pushing with the arms and not using the legs → The arms are just the connection; the push comes from your legs

ipuclari: Four cones in a T shape: run 10 m forward, shuffle 5 m left, shuffle 10 m right, shuffle 5 m left, backpedal to the start.
Don't cross your feet when shuffling; hips low, torso upright.
Start at 60–70% speed, then build up; 4–6 reps.
60–120 s full rest between reps.
hatalar: Crossing the feet → Shuffle without your feet touching
Stopping with straight knees → Slow down by bending your hips and knees before turning
Knee caving inward → Keep your knee in line with your foot

ipuclari: Start in the middle, run 5 m to one side and touch the line, 10 m to the other side, then 5 m back to the middle.
At the 180° turns, slow down over the last few steps, keep your hips low and push off the outside foot.
Learn it at a controlled speed first; 3–6 reps.
60–120 s between reps.
hatalar: Stopping stiff-legged at the turn → Slow down with short steps over the last 2–3 steps
Knee caving inward → Knee in line with your foot, torso facing the direction of the turn
Bending the torso excessively to touch the line → Squat down from your hips and knees

ipuclari: Start with simple patterns (one foot in each square, two feet, two in–two out sideways).
Light, quick contacts on the balls of your feet; let your arms follow the rhythm.
Accuracy first, then speed; 4–8 runs.
Use it as part of a warm-up or technique session.
hatalar: Looking at the floor and folding the torso forward → Eyes forward, torso upright
Tripping on the rungs → Slow down and memorise the pattern
Landing on the heels → Land on the balls of your feet

ipuclari: Start with 45° cuts; move on to 90° and 180° later.
Slow down in the steps before the cut; cutting foot wide, hips low, knee over your foot.
Torso upright and facing the new direction; don't lean too far to the side.
First change direction around cones, then reactively (to a signal).
4–8 reps, 60–120 s between reps.
hatalar: Knee caving inward and planting a straight leg → Reduce the angle and speed; keep your knee bent and over your foot
Torso leaning outside the cutting foot → Keep your torso upright and facing the new direction
Lots of sharp cuts when tired → Few quality reps

ipuclari: In a half-squat stance, shuffle sideways without crossing your feet.
Step with the lead foot and push with the trailing foot; your feet may come close but shouldn't touch.
5–10 m there and back, 3–6 reps; increase your speed over time.
hatalar: Standing up tall → Hips low, chest forward
Clicking the feet together → Keep your feet close to shoulder width
Knee caving inward → Keep your knee in line with your foot

ipuclari: Basketball defensive stance: feet wider than your shoulders, hips low, arms out.
Take a wide step with the lead foot and push with the trailing foot; keep your head height constant.
When changing direction, slow down first and push off the outside foot; progress by changing direction on a signal.
20–30 s work, 30–60 s rest, 4–8 reps.
hatalar: Head and hips bobbing up and down → Slide at the same height
Bringing the feet together → Wide base
Knee caving inward → Knee over your foot

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). Walk briskly: your breathing speeds up but you can still talk.
Start with 10-min bouts and build up to 30 min a day, 5 days a week.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
Comfortable shoes; move from flat ground to inclines.
hatalar: Walking too slowly → Use the talk test: you can talk but not sing
Overstriding → Take quicker steps
Increasing the duration quickly despite pain → Increase the duration gradually

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). Run at a pace where you can talk; if you can't, slow down or walk.
Beginners: first build up to 30 min of continuous running with run-walk intervals (Couch to 5K).
3 runs a week, with a rest day between them.
Increasing your step rate a little (5–10%) reduces the load on your knees.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
hatalar: Suddenly increasing the long-run distance → Keep any single run at most 10% longer than your longest run of the last 30 days
Running every run fast → Run most of your runs at a pace where you can talk
Landing with the foot far in front of the body (overstriding) → Increase your step rate by 5–10%

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification).
Walk for 5 min to warm up, then build up to your running pace; walk for 3–5 min at the end.
A 1% incline gives an effort close to running outdoors (expert consensus).
Run in the middle of the belt without holding on; choose your speed with the talk test, not the console display.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
hatalar: Suddenly increasing the long-run distance → Keep any single run at most 10% longer than your longest run of the last 30 days
Running every run fast → Run most of your runs at a pace where you can talk
Landing with the foot far in front of the body (overstriding) → Increase your step rate by 5–10%
Holding on to the handrails while running → Lower the speed and run freely
Getting too close to the front of the belt → Stay in the middle of the belt and attach the emergency stop clip

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification).
Saddle height: your knee should stay slightly bent when the pedal is at the bottom.
Moderate-to-high cadence (about 80–90 rpm) and moderate resistance; don't strain your knees with a heavy gear.
20–60 min; increase your weekly time gradually.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
hatalar: Low cadence at very heavy resistance → Reduce the resistance and increase the cadence
Saddle too low or too high → Set it so your knee is slightly bent at the bottom
Rounded back and neck reaching forward for long periods → Adjust the handlebar height and change position now and then

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). In water, heart rate may be slightly lower than on land at the same effort; talking and perceived effort are better guides (expert consensus).
Body straight and close to the surface; to breathe, rotate with your body instead of lifting your head.
Start with 25–50 m repeats with rest in between; then build up to continuous swimming.
Don't increase your weekly distance suddenly; reduce the volume if your shoulder hurts.
hatalar: Lifting the head to breathe → Turn your head to the side to breathe
Hand crossing the midline as it enters the water → Enter the water with your hand in line with your shoulder
Increasing the volume quickly → Increase your weekly distance gradually

ipuclari: Sequence: legs push → torso leans slightly back → arms pull; on the return, reverse it: arms → torso → legs.
Most of the power comes from your legs; back neutral, hinge from the hips.
Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). 10–30 min continuous or 250–500 m intervals.
Damper (air setting) at a medium level; a high damper doesn't mean a better workout.
hatalar: Lower back rounding, especially at the start of the stroke → Chest open, hinge from the hips; reduce the intensity when fatigued
Pulling with the arms first → Push with your legs first
Bending the knees before the arms on the return → Bend your knees once your arms have passed them

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification).
Stand tall and keep your heels on the pedals; don't put your weight on the handles.
Increase the resistance first, then the speed; 20–45 min.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
hatalar: Leaning on the handles → Hold them lightly, torso upright
Rising onto the toes → Keep your heels on the pedals
Resistance too low → Set the resistance using the talk test

ipuclari: Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). Stairs quickly push you into high intensity; choose your pace with the talk test.
Stand tall, put your whole foot on the step and push from your hips.
Start with 10–15 min and build up to 20–30 min.
Weekly target: 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous intensity, or a mix (WHO 2020).
hatalar: Hanging on the handles and leaning the torso forward → Hold lightly or let go, torso upright
Stepping only on the toes → Step with your whole foot
Knee caving inward → Keep your knee in line with your foot

ipuclari: Jump low (2–3 cm) on the balls of your feet; turn the rope with your wrists, arms close to your body.
Start with 30 s jumping / 30 s rest, 5–10 min in total; then extend the time.
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax). For long continuous jumping, drop to moderate intensity.
Non-slip, slightly forgiving surface; avoid concrete and asphalt.
Advanced skills like double unders increase the load on the ankles; add them gradually.
hatalar: Jumping high → Jump only high enough for the rope to pass
Landing on the heels → Land on the balls of your feet
Increasing the volume quickly → Increase your weekly time gradually; watch for pain the next day

ipuclari: Couch to 5K start: 5 min warm-up walk, then 1 min running / 1.5 min walking, 20 min in total.
Over 9 weeks, lengthen the running parts until you reach 30 min of continuous running.
3 sessions a week, with rest days in between.
Intensity: moderate (you can talk but not sing; about 64–76% HRmax, ACSM 2011 classification). Run the running parts at a pace where you can talk.
hatalar: Running the running parts too fast → Run at a pace where you can talk
Skipping weeks and progressing quickly → Repeat a week if you struggle
Continuing while pain increases → If pain is worse the next day, go back a step

ipuclari: Warm up with 5–10 min of easy running.
Example: 1–4 min fast (about 85–95% HRmax) / 1–3 min easy running or walking, 4–8 reps.
Example format: go up from a set speed to a higher one, then recover at a lower speed (e.g. up to 12 km/h, down to 9 km/h); choose your speeds based on your own talk test.
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax). In the fast part, you can't say more than a few words.
At most 1–2 interval sessions a week; easy days in between.
hatalar: Going into the fast part without warming up → Warm up gradually
Making every session an interval session → 1–2 sessions a week; most runs easy
Holding on to the handrails in the fast part → Lower the speed
Suddenly increasing the total distance in one session → Don't go more than 10% beyond your longest run of the last 30 days

ipuclari: Warm up for 10–15 min; first reps at 80% speed.
Example: 20–35 s fast running / 60–120 s walking, 4–10 reps.
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax). The fast part is near-maximal; you can't talk.
At most 1–2 sessions a week; fatigue can last up to 72 hours after sprinting.
hatalar: Going to full speed without warming up → Gradual warm-up and acceleration
Cutting the rest short and letting technique break down → Stop when speed or technique drops
Hard surface and poor shoes → Track, grass or treadmill

ipuclari: Squat down, put your hands on the floor, jump your legs back into a plank, (push-up), bring your feet back to your hands, jump up.
Beginner version: no push-up and no jump, stepping back and forward one foot at a time.
20–40 s work / 20–60 s rest, 4–8 rounds.
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax).
hatalar: Hips dropping in the plank → Abs tight, body straight
Landing hard when fatigued → Drop the jump or land softly
Slapping the hands onto the floor → Place your hands under control

ipuclari: In a high plank with your shoulders over your wrists; pull your knees to your chest one at a time.
Hips level with your shoulders; go from slow to fast.
20–40 s work / 20–40 s rest, 3–6 rounds.
hatalar: Raising the hips into the air → Hips level with your shoulders
Lower back sagging → Abs tight
Shoulders staying behind the hands → Bring your shoulders over your hands

ipuclari: Jump your feet apart and raise your arms overhead, then bring them back together.
Land softly on the balls of your feet; knees slightly bent.
For those who want to avoid impact, a stepping version (side step + arms).
20–60 s of work, in a warm-up or circuit.
hatalar: Landing hard on straight knees → Bend your knees slightly
Knees caving inward → Knees in line with your feet as your feet open

ipuclari: Half-squat stance, chest open; make waves with the ropes alternately or together.
The movement comes from your shoulders and arms; torso still.
20–30 s work / 30–60 s rest, 4–8 rounds.
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax).
hatalar: Folding forward at the waist → Hips back, chest up, abs tight
Shrugging the shoulders to the ears → Keep your shoulders down
Locking the knees → Knees slightly bent

ipuclari: Warm up with 5 min of easy pedalling.
Beginner: 20–30 s high effort / 60–120 s very easy, 4–8 rounds; advanced: 30 s / 30 s or Tabata (20/10).
Intensity: vigorous (you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath; about 77–95% HRmax). Because resistance rises quickly, you reach maximal effort in a short time.
Finish with 3–5 min of easy pedalling; don't stop abruptly.
hatalar: Full effort without warming up → Warm up gradually
Stopping abruptly and sitting/lying down straight away → Cool down with easy pedalling
Wrong saddle setting → Knee slightly bent at the bottom

ekipman.ayakta baldır makinesi ya da leg press: standing calf machine or leg press
ekipman.barfiks barı ve lastik bant ya da destek: pull-up bar and resistance band, or assisted pull-up machine
ekipman.bloklar ya da squat sehpasının alt pimle: blocks or the low pins of a squat rack
ekipman.landmine ya da köşeye dayalı barbell: landmine or a barbell wedged in a corner
ekipman.tek elle tutulabilen hafif sağlık topu: light medicine ball you can hold in one hand
ekipman.topuk sabitleme (Nordic aparatı, makine: heel anchor (Nordic bench, machine pad or a partner)
ekipman.önde sabit bağlantı noktası: fixed anchor point in front of you

1–2.name: Foundation
1–2.txt: Learn the movements. In every set, use a weight that leaves at least 3 more reps in the tank. Take your baseline measurements before the first workout of week 1.

3–4.name: Strength I
3–4.txt: Main lifts go up to 4 sets. If you hit the target reps on every set in a session, add 2.5–5% to the weight next time.

5–6.name: Strength II
5–6.txt: Heavier, fewer reps. The Zercher and the sandbag get heavier. On the lat pulldown, if you finished every set at the target reps while leaving 2 in reserve (RIR 2), add one weight step next session.

7.name: Deload week
7.txt: Fewer sets, weights about 85% of week 6. Your body recovers and gets stronger this week; don't skip it.

8–9.name: Power I
8–9.txt: The approach jump replaces the single-leg hop, and contact landings begin. Do explosive movements at maximum speed on every rep; end the set when the speed drops.

10–11.name: Power II
10–11.txt: The heaviest strength sets (5×3) and the highest jump volume. Don't let sleep and calories slip during these two weeks.

12.name: Peak and test
12.txt: Volume drops by about half. On day A test your trap bar 3-rep max, on day B measure your jump-and-touch, and see where you are on the dunk ladder.

isinma.title: Warm-up
isinma.sub: 10 minutes, before every workout. Then warm-up sets for the first heavy lift: empty bar, then 3, 2 and 1 reps at 50%, 70% and 85%.

1:askip.cue: Pull the knee to hip height, toes point up, the opposite arm swings forward.

2:legswing.cue: Hold a wall with one hand. Torso upright, let the swing come from the hip.

3:ankle.cue: Front foot a hand's width from the wall. Without lifting the heel, touch your knee to the wall.

4:lunge.cue: Take 3 seconds to lower on the step back. As you rise, drive the back knee toward your chest and hold your balance for 1 second.

5:bridge.cue: Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes at the top. Lift with your hips, not your lower back.

6:squatjump.cue: Land quietly and hold still for 2 seconds. Knees over your toes, not caving in.

gunA.title: Lift and press
gunA.sub: Hip power, pressing strength, trunk stiffness. About 60–70 minutes.

A1:boxjump.cue: Jump onto a 40–50 cm box, land quietly, then step down. Don't jump back down off the box.
A1:boxjump.alt: No box: squat jumps in place

A2:trapbar.cue: Push your hips back, chest up. Push the floor away with your feet; the handles rise alongside your legs.

A3:bench.cue: Squeeze your shoulder blades and lower the bar to mid-chest. Elbows about 45° from your torso.

A4:dbrow.cue: A separate set for each arm. Pull your elbow toward your hip, don't rotate your torso.

A5a:nordic.cue: Knees on the pad, heels anchored. Body straight, fall forward as slowly as you can, catch yourself with your hands and push back up.

A5b:revnordic.cue: Knees on the floor, torso and thighs in one line. Lean back slowly and come back with your quads. If your knee hurts, shorten the range.

A6:pallof.cue: Stand side-on to a cable machine. Press the handle straight out from your chest and hold. The cable tries to rotate you; you don't let it.

A7:farmer.cue: Walk tall with two heavy dumbbells. Shoulders down, steps short and quick.

gunB.title: Jump and pull
gunB.sub: Jumping and landing technique, single-leg strength, back and shoulders. At least 48 hours before a game.

B1:hopstick.cue: Hop forward on one leg, land on the same leg and hold still for 3 seconds. If your knee caves in, shorten the distance.
B1:hopstick.alt: Also do lateral hop and stick at the same dose

B1:approach.cue: Approach in 2–3 steps, lower over the last two, jump off both feet and land softly on both. Rest 45–60 seconds between reps.
B1:approach.alt: No hoop: jump and reach on a wall

B2:kbswing.cue: Hinge at the hips; the kettlebell passes between your legs. Drive your hips forward explosively, the arms just carry it.
B2:kbswing.alt: Alternative: trap bar jump (20–30% of your deadlift max)

B3:goblet.cue: Dumbbell at your chest, elbows travel down between your knees. Go as deep as you can without pain.

B3:frontsquat.cue: Bar in front of your collarbones, elbows high. Descend with an upright torso; the front knee may travel toward your toes.
B3:frontsquat.alt: Alternative: stay with the goblet squat

B4:latpull.cue: Lock your knees under the pad, grip the bar a little wider than shoulder width. Lift your chest, lean back slightly; pull the bar to your collarbone, elbows down and back. Let it up over 2 seconds and straighten your arms fully at the top.

B5:bss.cue: Back foot on the bench. Keep the front knee in line with your 2nd and 3rd toes. Lower until the back knee nears the floor.

B6:ohp.cue: Brace your abs and glutes, don't arch your lower back. Bring the dumbbells together overhead.

B7:mbpass.cue: From 2–3 m away from a wall, throw with both hands like a chest pass. Push off the back foot; every rep at maximum speed.
B7:mbpass.alt: Alternative: chest pass with a partner

B8:copenhagen.cue: Side plank with the top leg on the bench. Lift the bottom leg up to the bench. In the first weeks keep your knee on the bench.

B9:contact.cue: While you are in the air, your partner pushes your chest or shoulder with a pad. Brace your trunk and land balanced on both feet.
B9:contact.alt: No partner: catch a medicine ball in the air and land

gunC.title: Contact and upper body
gunC.sub: Full-body strength, arm and shoulder size, heavy carries. "a" and "b" movements are supersets: do them back to back, then rest.

C1:slam.cue: Lift the ball overhead and, bracing your abs, slam it into the floor as hard as you can. Squat down to pick it up.

C2:zercher.cue: Set the bar at mid-shin height: blocks or the low pins of a rack. Starting from the floor overloads the knee and lower back. Squat down, take the bar into the crook of your elbows, clasp your hands in front of your chest. Chest up, back flat; stand up by extending hips and knees together. Keep the bar close to your body. Wrap a towel or pad around the elbow crease.

C3:incline.cue: Bench at 30°. Lower the dumbbells to your upper chest and bring them together at the top.

C4:cablerow.cue: Chest up, pull the handle to your stomach, squeeze your shoulder blades together. Return forward with little torso sway.

C5a:curl.cue: Elbows fixed at your sides. Turn the wrist out as you lift, lower over 3 seconds.

C5b:hammer.cue: Palms face each other. Also strengthens the forearm and grip, which helps ball control.

C6a:facepull.cue: Pull the rope to your face, elbows high and back. For the health of your shooting shoulder.

C6b:slcalf.cue: On a step, lower the heel and pause 1 second. Rise onto your toes and hold 1 second.

C7:bearhug.cue: Hug the bag to your chest and walk tall with short steps. Breathe under control.

soguma.title: Cool-down
soguma.sub: 5 minutes. Slow your breathing; don't push a stretch into pain.

1:hipflexor.cue: Half-kneel, squeeze your glute and shift your hips slightly forward. Reach the same-side arm overhead.

2:hamstr.cue: Front leg straight, heel down, toes up. Keeping your back flat, lean forward from the hips.

3:calfwall.cue: Back leg straight, heel down. Lean your hands on the wall and push your hips forward.

dereceler.akut: Pain lasting less than 6 weeks. Most people improve noticeably within the first 6 weeks.
dereceler.subakut: Pain lasting 6–12 weeks. Improvement slows down.
dereceler.kronik: Longer than 12 weeks. Low-to-moderate pain may persist for a year; scored by pain rather than duration.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Cauda equina: new inability to hold or pass urine, faecal incontinence, numbness in the saddle area, weakness in both legs → emergency.
Progressive leg weakness or loss of sensation.
History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, pain at night and at rest that doesn't ease.
Fever, recent infection, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression (suspected infection).
Major trauma, osteoporosis or long-term corticosteroid use (suspected fracture).
Recent invasive procedure on the lower back.

dereceler.hafif: Pain radiating into the leg, no loss of strength. Most people recover without surgery.
dereceler.orta: Marked leg pain and numbness; daily tasks become harder.
dereceler.siddetli: Loss of strength (e.g. unable to lift the ankle) or unbearable pain; needs surgical assessment.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Urinary or faecal incontinence, numbness in the saddle area, symptoms in both legs (cauda equina) → emergency department.
Rapidly progressing weakness (foot drop, unable to rise onto your toes).
Fever, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss.
Severe leg pain lasting beyond 6–12 weeks despite non-surgical treatment → surgical opinion.

dereceler.hafif: Pain related to posture or strain that changes with movement.
dereceler.siddetli: Severe pain when breathing or at rest; red flags must be ruled out first.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating, pain spreading to the arm or jaw (may be cardiac) → emergency.
Sudden, severe, tearing back pain (aorta) → emergency.
The thoracic region is a warning sign in itself for serious spinal pathology: history of cancer, weight loss, night pain.
Pain after osteoporosis, corticosteroid use or trauma (fracture).
Fever or new weakness and unsteadiness in the legs (spinal cord compression).

dereceler.hafif_alevlenme: Pain after long walks or stairs; settles quickly.
dereceler.orta_alevlenme: Pain and morning stiffness that limit daily activities; there may be swelling.
dereceler.siddetli_alevlenme: Pain at rest, marked swelling; bearing load is difficult.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Hot, red, very swollen knee with fever (infection or crystal arthritis) → see a doctor the same day.
Unable to bear weight after trauma (Ottawa knee rule: over 55, isolated tenderness at the fibular head or patella, unable to bend to 90°, unable to take 4 steps) → X-ray.
Locking or frequent giving way (meniscus or ligament).

dereceler.hafif: Pain only after prolonged sitting, going down stairs or running.
dereceler.orta: Pain during squats, stairs and running; training should be modified.
dereceler.siddetli: Pain during everyday walking, ongoing for a long time.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Marked swelling, locking or giving way (not expected in patellofemoral pain) → another diagnosis.
Unable to bear weight after trauma (Ottawa knee rule).
In children and adolescents, possible knee pain referred from the hip (examine the hip).

dereceler.evre_1_izometrik: Pain is high; jumping is painful. Pain-relieving isometric loading (e.g. 5×45 s wall sit or leg extension hold).
dereceler.evre_2_izotonik: Pain is manageable; heavy slow resistance (leg press, squat, leg extension) is added.
dereceler.evre_3_enerji_depolama: Tolerates heavy load; jumping and landing are added gradually.
dereceler.evre_4_spora_donus: Return to sport-specific volume; tendon load is monitored week by week.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A sudden 'pop' with a gap at the front of the knee and inability to raise the straight leg (tendon rupture) → emergency.
Hot, red swelling and fever.
In adolescents, pain at the tibial tuberosity (Osgood-Schlatter) is assessed separately.

dereceler.1: Mild damage to the ligament, no laxity.
dereceler.3_ameliyatsiz: Complete tear, non-surgical route: progressive rehabilitation; return is mostly to straight-line sports (swimming, cycling, running).
dereceler.3_ameliyatli: Complete tear and reconstruction. Returning before month 9 increases the risk of re-injury.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A 'pop' at the moment of injury and rapid swelling within the first hours (bleeding into the joint) → doctor.
Knee giving way or locking (associated meniscal tear).
Positive Ottawa knee rule (over 55, tenderness at the fibular head or patella, unable to bend to 90°, unable to take 4 steps) → X-ray.
Swelling and pain in the calf or numbness in the foot (neurovascular injury, clot) → emergency.

dereceler.dejeneratif: A tear with gradual onset in middle age and older; first-line treatment is exercise, arthroscopy is not recommended.
dereceler.travmatik_ameliyatsiz: A stable tear that doesn't cause locking; managed with exercise.
dereceler.menisektomi_sonrasi: Arthroscopic removal of the torn fragment; most people return to previous activity in 4–5 weeks.
dereceler.onarim_sonrasi: Meniscal repair; return to sport at 22–27 weeks, longer for complex and lateral meniscus tears.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Locked knee: unable to fully straighten the knee and it gets stuck → orthopaedics.
Rapid swelling immediately after injury (may come with an ACL tear).
Hot, red knee and fever.

dereceler.1: Mild damage and pain; no laxity (3–5 mm opening).
dereceler.2: Partial tear; laxity with the knee bent to 30° (6–10 mm).
dereceler.3: Complete tear; laxity with the knee straight too (>10 mm). Often combined with another ligament injury; sometimes surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Laxity with the knee straight too, or signs of an associated ACL tear (pop, rapid swelling).
Positive Ottawa knee rule → X-ray.
Locking (meniscus).

dereceler.hafif: Outer knee pain that starts towards the end of a long run.
dereceler.orta: Starts in the first kilometres of a run and stops the run.
dereceler.siddetli: Pain when walking and on stairs too.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Swelling, locking or laxity (lateral meniscus or ligament).
Pain after trauma.

dereceler.hafif_alevlenme: Groin pain after long walks, morning stiffness.
dereceler.orta_alevlenme: Putting on shoes and getting up from a chair are painful.
dereceler.siddetli_alevlenme: Pain at rest and at night; limping.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Hip pain after a fall and inability to bear weight (hip fracture) → emergency.
Fever and a hot, very painful joint (infection).
New groin pain in a young person who uses corticosteroids or alcohol (avascular necrosis).
Groin pain that worsens with load in a runner (femoral neck stress fracture) → same-day assessment.

dereceler.hafif: Pain on the outside of the hip after long walks or when lying on your side.
dereceler.orta: Pain on stairs, when standing on one leg and at night.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Unable to bear weight after a fall (fracture).
If groin pain and loss of internal rotation dominate, consider arthritis or an intra-articular problem.
Fever, redness and warmth (infected bursitis).

dereceler.1: Functional disorder or small partial tear; painful but walking is normal.
dereceler.2: Moderate partial tear; bringing the legs together and running are painful.
dereceler.3: Near-complete or complete tear, proximal avulsion.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Suspected avulsion: sudden severe pain, large bruise, unable to bring the leg in.
Swelling in the groin or a lump that grows when you cough (hernia).
Deep groin pain that worsens with load in a runner (femoral neck or pubic stress fracture).
Fever, urinary complaints (internal organ pain referred to the groin).

dereceler.1: Functional disorder or small partial tear; pulling the knee to the chest is painful.
dereceler.2: Moderate partial tear; running and kicking are painful.
dereceler.3: Near-complete/complete tear or avulsion (in adolescents, pulling away from a bony prominence).

kirmizi_bayraklar: Sudden groin pain and inability to walk in an adolescent (apophyseal avulsion) → X-ray.
Groin pain that worsens with load in a runner (femoral neck stress fracture).
Fever or abdominal pain (psoas abscess, appendicitis).

dereceler.0: No findings on MRI; functional disorder (Munich type 1–2).
dereceler.1: Oedema on MRI, no fibre disruption; borderline minor partial tear (Munich 3A).

kirmizi_bayraklar: Suspected proximal avulsion: a 'pop' at the sitting bone, large bruise, unable to walk, palpable gap → early orthopaedic referral (timing of surgery matters).
Numbness and tingling spreading down the leg (radiculopathy from the lower back).
Swelling and pain that grow without a blow (compartment syndrome, clot).

dereceler.1: Functional disorder, small partial tear or mild contusion; the knee bends beyond 90°.
dereceler.2: Moderate partial tear or moderate contusion; limping, knee bending limited.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Increasing swelling, tightness and pain after a contusion (compartment syndrome) → emergency.
A lump that hardens and doesn't go away 2–3 weeks after a contusion (myositis ossificans).
Palpable gap and inability to straighten the knee (complete tear).

dereceler.1: Functional disorder or small partial tear; walking is mildly painful.
dereceler.2: Moderate partial tear; rising onto your toes is painful.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A 'pop' near the heel, unable to do a single-leg heel raise, positive Thompson test (Achilles rupture) → emergency.
Swelling, warmth and redness without a blow, after a long journey or immobility (deep vein thrombosis) → emergency.
Increasing hardness and pain (compartment syndrome).

dereceler.reaktif_yuksek_agri: Marked pain and morning stiffness after a recent increase in load. Reduce load; isometrics and light calf raises.
dereceler.yuk_toleransi: Pain is manageable; heavy slow or eccentric calf raises. Improvement starts from week 2; by week 12 VISA-A rises by 18–21 points.
dereceler.enerji_depolama_ve_kosu: Jumping, fast running and sport-specific load are added.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A sudden 'pop', feeling of being kicked, unable to do a single-leg heel raise (rupture) → emergency.
Tendon pain that started after a fluoroquinolone antibiotic.
Tendon pain on both sides with joint swelling (rheumatic disease).
Bone tenderness in the heel (stress fracture).

dereceler.kismi: Partial rupture; early protection with a boot or cast.
dereceler.tam_ameliyatsiz: Complete rupture, non-surgical treatment with a functional boot and early movement; treatment takes 6–12 months.
dereceler.tam_ameliyatli: Complete rupture, repair; 6 weeks in a boot. Light running at weeks 12–16, non-contact sport at 16–20, contact sport at 20–24.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Suspected rupture needs a doctor in itself: a pop, feeling of being kicked, unable to rise onto your toes, a gap in the tendon.
Swelling and pain in the calf during the boot period (deep vein thrombosis) → emergency.
Wound discharge or fever (post-operative infection).

dereceler.1: Mild damage to the ligaments and pain; no laxity.
dereceler.2: More ligament damage, mild laxity in the joint.
dereceler.3: Ligament completely torn, joint very lax. If needed, a cast or rigid support for up to 10 days.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Ottawa ankle rules: unable to take 4 steps both immediately and at examination, tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of the malleoli, at the base of the 5th metatarsal or at the navicular → X-ray.
Pain above the ankle between the two bones, worse with external rotation (syndesmosis).
Deformity, numbness or coldness in the foot → emergency.
Deep joint pain and catching that persist for weeks (osteochondral lesion).

dereceler.stabil: Damage to the syndesmotic ligament but no widening of the joint; non-surgical.
dereceler.instabil: Ligament torn, widening between the tibia and fibula; often surgery (fixation).

kirmizi_bayraklar: Positive Ottawa rules or pain in the upper fibula (Maisonneuve fracture) → X-ray.
Unable to bear weight with marked swelling; painful squeeze and external rotation tests → imaging.
Deformity, numbness in the foot.

dereceler.hafif: Occasional feeling of giving way; apprehension during sport (CAIT ≤25).
dereceler.orta: Recurrent sprains; unsteadiness during everyday walking.
dereceler.siddetli: Frequent giving way despite exercise; surgical assessment.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Deep joint pain, catching and swelling (osteochondral lesion, impingement) → imaging.
Frequent giving way despite an exercise programme → orthopaedics.
Positive Ottawa rules after a new sprain.

dereceler.hafif: Heel pain with the first steps in the morning; eases during the day.
dereceler.orta: Pain with prolonged standing and walking too.
dereceler.siddetli: Pain that lasts all day; ongoing for months.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Pain when squeezing the heel from both sides and pain that worsens with load (calcaneal stress fracture).
Burning, numbness, tingling (tarsal tunnel, nerve entrapment).
Heel pain on both sides with morning stiffness, together with back/joint pain (rheumatic disease).
Night pain, fever.

dereceler.siddetli: Pain when walking and at rest.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Sharp bone pain at a single spot you can point to with a finger, night pain or pain when hopping on one leg (stress fracture) → imaging.
A feeling of tightness and numbness that builds during exercise and goes away with rest (compartment syndrome).
Menstrual irregularity and low energy intake in a female athlete (bone health risk).

stres_kirigi_alt.ad: Lower limb bone stress injury (tibia, metatarsal)

dereceler.dusuk_riskli: Low-risk sites such as the posteromedial tibial shaft, fibula, 2nd–4th metatarsals. Reduce load and return gradually.
dereceler.yuksek_riskli: Navicular, femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, base of the 5th metatarsal. High risk of complications; often non-weight-bearing or surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Bone tenderness at a single spot, pain at night and at rest, unable to hop on one leg → imaging (X-ray may be normal early on; MRI).
A runner with groin or hip pain (femoral neck) → same-day assessment, stop weight-bearing.
Pain on top of the midfoot (navicular) or at the base of the 5th metatarsal (high risk).
Recurrent stress fractures, menstrual irregularity, low energy intake (REDs) → sports physician.

dereceler.hafif: Stiffness and pain in the neck, movement largely free, no spread into the arm.
dereceler.orta: Marked restriction of movement, daily tasks are a struggle; no spread into the arm.
dereceler.kola_yayilan: Pain spreads into the arm, with numbness or tingling (suspected radiculopathy).

kirmizi_bayraklar: Neck pain that started after a fall, accident or blow (needs screening for fracture / ligament instability).
Clumsiness in both hands, unsteadiness when walking, altered sensation in the legs (suspected spinal cord compression / myelopathy).
Neck and head pain together with dizziness, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, sudden falls, facial numbness, nausea (suspected neck artery problem; emergency).
Progressive weakness in the arm or spreading loss of sensation.
Fever, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer or night pain that doesn't ease with rest.
Pain doesn't settle within a few weeks or gets worse despite painkillers.

dereceler.evre_1: Pain only after demanding shoulder work (stage of oedema and minor bleeding).
dereceler.evre_2: Pain with any activity; tendinopathy, small tears.
dereceler.evre_3_kismi_yirtik: Pain at rest too; partial-thickness tear or bony changes.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Unable to lift the arm or sudden weakness after a fall or sudden pull (acute tear; prompt referral).
Obvious deformity, fever or chills.
Chest pain, shortness of breath or left shoulder pain that comes on with exertion (cardiovascular or visceral pain).
History or suspicion of cancer, unexplained weight loss.
Pain and numbness spreading from the neck into the arm (may come from the neck; screen the neck).
Severe, persistent pain or restriction despite 12 weeks of appropriate treatment (see a specialist).

dereceler.kismi_kalinlik: Part of the tendon is torn; managed like tendinopathy.
dereceler.akut_travmatik_ya_da_ameliyatli: Large traumatic full-thickness tear or after repair surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Sudden weakness and inability to lift the arm after a fall, dislocation or heavy lift (acute traumatic tear; prompt orthopaedic referral).
Over 40, unable to lift the arm or weak external rotation after a shoulder dislocation.
Pain or weakness steadily getting worse (the tear may be growing).
Fever, red and hot joint, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss.
Pain and loss of function persisting despite 6–12 months of non-surgical treatment (surgical assessment).

dereceler.kismi_cikik: The shoulder came out and went back in by itself (subluxation); laxity and pain.
dereceler.ilk_tam_cikik: First complete dislocation, reduced, non-surgical treatment.
dereceler.tekrarlayan_ya_da_ameliyatli: Recurrent instability or after stabilisation surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: The shoulder hasn't gone back in: emergency department the same day (BESS/BOA, TSHD). Even if you put it back yourself, you need an examination and X-ray.
Loss of sensation on the outer shoulder or unable to lift the arm to the side (axillary nerve injury).
Over 40, weakness after a dislocation (rotator cuff tear in ~40%; imaging).
Suspected fracture: severe trauma, pain over the bone, deformity.
Fever and a hot, red joint (infection; same day).
The shoulder keeps dislocating or constantly feels like it's slipping (surgical assessment).

dereceler.donma_evresi: Stage 1–2: sharp pain at end range, night and rest pain, restriction setting in (high irritability).
dereceler.donmus_evre: Stage 3: stiffness dominates, pain is easing.
dereceler.cozulme_evresi: Stage 4: movement slowly returns, little pain.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Fever, red and hot shoulder (joint infection).
Restriction that started after a fall or blow (fracture or dislocation must be ruled out).
History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, constant night pain.
Left shoulder pain with exertion, chest pain or shortness of breath.
Suspected diabetes or thyroid problem (blood sugar and thyroid check recommended).
Pain severe enough to stop you moving the arm (see a doctor).

dereceler.tip_2: AC ligament completely torn, coracoclavicular ligament sprained; slight step.
dereceler.tip_3: Coracoclavicular ligament completely torn; clavicle 25–100% higher.
dereceler.tip_4_6: Clavicle displaced backwards, far upwards or downwards; surgery is the priority.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Obvious step, clavicle displaced backwards or skin tenting (types 4–6; surgeon).
Bone tenderness along the clavicle, crepitus (fracture; X-ray).
Numbness, weakness or coldness in the arm.
Pain when breathing or shortness of breath (chest trauma).
Pain and loss of function persisting despite non-surgical treatment (surgical assessment for type 3).

dereceler.yeni_baslayan: Front-of-shoulder pain with activity, lasting for weeks.
dereceler.uzun_suren: Pain lasting for months or with an associated shoulder problem.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A sudden 'pop' with a 'Popeye' bulge at the front of the arm and bruising (tendon rupture).
Sudden pain and pop at the front of the elbow, weak elbow bending (distal biceps rupture; prompt orthopaedic referral).
A feeling of the shoulder slipping or coming out (instability / labrum).
Fever, night pain, history of cancer.

dereceler.suregen: Pain lasting for months (subacute or chronic).

kirmizi_bayraklar: Swelling, deformity or inability to fully straighten and bend the elbow after a fall or blow (fracture / instability).
Locking or catching in the elbow (intra-articular problem).
Pain and numbness spreading from the neck into the arm (cervical radiculopathy must be ruled out).
Unable to straighten the fingers or loss of sensation on the back of the hand (nerve entrapment).
Fever, red and hot elbow.
Numbness in the ring and little fingers or weakness in the hand (ulnar nerve / cubital tunnel).
A 'pop' on the inside of the elbow while throwing, followed by weakness or laxity (medial collateral ligament injury).
Swelling, deformity, inability to fully straighten and bend after a fall.
Fever, red and hot elbow.

dereceler.2: Ligament partially torn; a splint or cast may be needed.
dereceler.3: Ligament completely torn; needs medical or surgical treatment.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Tenderness at the base of the thumb (anatomical snuffbox): treat as a scaphoid fracture, immobilise and image (X-ray may be normal in the first days).
Obvious deformity, unable to bear weight, point tenderness over the bone (fracture / dislocation).
Sudden numbness or tingling, suddenly increasing pain or swelling, locking in the wrist (MedlinePlus).
No expected improvement within 1–2 weeks (further tests for ligament injury / instability).

dereceler.hafif_aralikli: Numbness and tingling that come and go, worse at night.
dereceler.orta_surekli: Numbness that persists during the day too, difficulty gripping.
dereceler.agir_ya_da_ameliyat: Muscle wasting, permanent loss of sensation; the period after surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Muscle wasting at the base of the thumb, dropping things, marked weakness (advanced compression).
Permanent loss of sensation.
Numbness that starts rapidly after a wrist fracture or major trauma (emergency).
Numbness spreading into the arm with neck pain, or clumsiness in both hands (may come from the neck).
Getting worse despite home treatment.

dereceler.yeni_baslayan: Thumb-side wrist pain lasting for weeks.
dereceler.suregen: Pain lasting longer than 6 weeks or recurring.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Pain at the base of the thumb after a fall (scaphoid fracture must be ruled out).
Redness, marked swelling and fever (infection).
Numbness in the thumb and back of the hand (nerve involvement).
No improvement within 6 weeks despite a splint, ice and medication (see a doctor).

dereceler.1: Mild strain of the muscle fibres; little loss of strength, no deformity.
dereceler.2: Partial tear in the muscle belly; marked pain, loss of strength, bruising.
dereceler.3: Complete rupture of the tendon or musculotendinous junction; usually surgery.

kirmizi_bayraklar: A 'pop' or tearing sensation during a lift, followed by loss of the front armpit fold and a dip in the chest (complete rupture; early surgical assessment, early repair gives better results).
Bruising from the front of the chest down the arm and weak internal rotation.
Chest pain during or after exertion, shortness of breath, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, sweating (may be cardiac; emergency).
Large and growing swelling (haematoma).

dereceler.hafif: Tender to touch and stretch; movement is comfortable.
dereceler.orta: Pain and stiffness with movement; tasks like going down stairs are uncomfortable.
dereceler.belirgin: Marked loss of strength and restricted movement, swelling.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Dark (tea- or cola-coloured) urine, excessive swelling or marked weakness (suspected rhabdomyolysis; emergency). Expert consensus.
Pain lasts longer than 7 days or gets worse as the days pass (not DOMS; a strain or another problem).
Pain started suddenly and sharply during exercise, with a 'pop' or bruising (muscle strain / tear).
Calf pain with swelling, redness and warmth in one leg that doesn't go away (suspected clot). Expert consensus.

dereceler.tek_kramp: A single cramp that goes with stretching; mild tenderness afterwards.
dereceler.kramp_sonrasi_agri: Pain and stiffness lasting 1–2 days after the cramp.
dereceler.tekrarlayan: Cramps that recur in the same session or over several days.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Cramp together with dizziness, fainting, nausea and vomiting, dark urine or altered consciousness: stop exercising, go to hospital (Miller 2022).
Headache, nausea, confusion during a long endurance event with high fluid intake (suspected low sodium; emergency).
Frequently recurring cramps or cramps that started after a new medication (medical assessment).
Swelling, bruising or a 'pop' feeling that persists after the cramp has passed (muscle tear).

dereceler.hafif: Normal walking, local tenderness; knee bends > 90°.
dereceler.orta: Limping, swollen and tender lump; knee bends 45–90°.
dereceler.siddetli: Marked limp, large swollen lump; knee bends < 45°.

kirmizi_bayraklar: Swelling that increases over hours, very hard and tight muscle, severe pain even at rest, numbness or a pale foot (compartment syndrome; emergency). Expert consensus.
Worsening after 2–3 weeks, decreasing knee bend and persistent swelling (myositis ossificans; imaging).
Large bruise with blood thinner use or a bleeding disorder.
Point tenderness over the bone or inability to bear weight (fracture).

parq: Has your doctor ever said that you have a heart condition OR high blood pressure?
Do you feel pain in your chest at rest, during your daily activities of living, OR when you do physical activity?
Do you lose balance because of dizziness OR have you lost consciousness in the last 12 months? (Answer NO if your dizziness was associated with over-breathing, including during vigorous exercise.)
Have you ever been diagnosed with another chronic medical condition (other than heart disease or high blood pressure)?
Are you currently taking prescribed medications for a chronic medical condition?

Do you currently have (or have had within the past 12 months) a bone, joint, or soft tissue (muscle, ligament, or tendon) problem that could be made worse by becoming more physically active? (Answer NO if you had a problem in the past, but it does not limit your current ability to be physically active.)
Has your doctor ever said that you should only do medically supervised physical activity?

1.tanim: No resistance training experience, or has taken a break of several years.

2.tanim: Has been doing regular resistance training for about 6 months.

3.tanim: Has years of regular resistance training experience.
